metadata.title: How Does Claude Build a Due Diligence Checklist?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude uses its own judgment to decide what belongs in a due diligence checklist -- or is doing something narrower. Lands the carry-out that the checklist tailors known workstreams to the deal's sector and type from a written file, and only escalates what it's already tracking.
metadata.source_note: NBB cut derived from the hai-simple (Plain) source. Facts preserved verbatim: the dd-checklist skill generates and tracks due diligence checklists tailored to the target's sector, deal type, and complexity; covers major workstreams with request lists, status tracking, and red-flag escalation; used when kicking off diligence, organizing a data room review, or tracking outstanding items. Register re-registered Plain -> Teardown; BHTF re-cast as the second-to-last LLM exercise beat (paste-ready prompt + dig-deeper); BOUT rebuilt as the NikBearBrown outro.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (a software acquisition's 'customer contracts' request traveling requested -> received -> reviewed -> flagged as a red flag, then paid off into 'run twice, same checklist' / 'a deal type outside the file has nothing tailored to reach for')

beats.narration_text: Someone asks whether Claude uses its own judgment to decide what belongs in a due diligence checklist. It doesn't. It reads a written file. Liam, in for Bear — let's take the skill apart, piece by piece.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What decides the checklist -- judgment?', hesitates on 'judgment', corrects to 'the file', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('judgment' -> 'the file') is visible on a late frame, fully settled before the beat ends.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess: Claude weighs this specific deal and decides, from its own judgment, which risks are worth chasing. Here's what's actually happening. It reads three inputs off the target — sector, deal type, complexity — and pulls workstreams from templates the file already defines. Request lists, status tracking, red-flag escalation, all pre-written. They optimized for auditable consistency at the expense of range: hand it a sector the file never lists and there's no independent research to reach for.

shot.new_visual_element: A deal-judgment figure weighing risks ad hoc, struck through; a sector/type/complexity-to-workstreams procedure card lit instead

production_viz.label: Deal judgment, struck -- sector/type/complexity, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'DEAL JUDGMENT' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered card labelled 'SECTOR + TYPE -> WORKSTREAMS' listing three steps: read sector/type/complexity, match workstream templates, build request lists. The judgment side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the procedure side stays lit. A final line reads 'sector not listed -- no template' and the figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. The skill reads the deal's sector, type, and complexity, then generates the workstreams that profile calls for — each carrying its own request list. Watch it on a software company acquisition. 'Customer contracts' goes out as a request, comes back received, gets reviewed — and one clause, heavy revenue concentration in a single customer, gets flagged for the deal team. Four states — requested, received, reviewed, flagged — because that's exactly what the file was built to track, and nothing beyond it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a 'customer contracts' request traveling requested -> received -> reviewed -> flagged

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one request, four stops
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked cards labelled 'REQUESTED', 'RECEIVED', 'REVIEWED', 'FLAGGED'. A single highlighted token 'CUSTOMER CONTRACTS' travels down through all four cards in turn, each lighting terracotta as it arrives. At the bottom, beside the FLAGGED card, a small note reads 'revenue concentration -- one customer' and the token halts there. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, CONDENSED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The flag reaches the deal team because the item was on the checklist to begin with. That's the design: escalate what's already tracked, never go looking beyond the list. Run the same software acquisition checklist twice and the workstreams and request items come back identical — which is what you want for reproducibility, and exactly what fails you if the checklist needed to catch something new. Ask for a deal type the file never described — a mineral rights transfer, say — and there's nothing tailored to reach for; the checklist stops exactly where SKILL.md stops. This works if you value consistent, auditable coverage of known workstreams. It fails if you need Claude to invent workstreams the file didn't teach it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, condensed; splits into 'run twice -- same checklist' and 'mineral rights transfer -- no template'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- run twice, or stops there
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 COMPOSITION RETURNS, condensed to a small resting row (RECEIVED / REVIEWED / FLAGGED). It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'RUN TWICE' then 'SAME CHECKLIST' with a checkmark, labelled 'same input, same checklist' (holds); right reads 'MINERAL RIGHTS TRANSFER' then a struck-through 'TAILORED?', labelled 'stops where the file does' (flips).

beats.narration_text: So: a Claude due diligence checklist isn't independent judgment about a deal's risks. It's a written procedure that tailors known workstreams to the deal's sector and type, and it only escalates what it's already tracking.

props.quote: A Claude due diligence checklist isn't independent judgment about a deal's risks — it's a written procedure that tailors known workstreams to the deal's sector and type, and it only escalates what it's already tracking.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it a deal profile — a software company acquisition, say — and ask it to walk the dd-checklist workflow: build the workstreams for that profile, the request lists inside each one, and where red-flag escalation would trigger. Then ask it for a deal type you never named — a mineral rights transfer — and see whether it invents new workstreams or admits the checklist stops where the file does. Go deeper: what would it take to add a new deal type to that skill — a whole new workstream template, or just one more line in the file? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how a due diligence checklist skill actually works when a language model runs it. Assume the skill reads the target's sector, deal type, and complexity, then pulls workstream templates from a written file (request lists, status tracking, red-flag escalation) rather than judging deal-specific risk from scratch. Give me a deal profile — a mid-market software company acquisition — and walk the dd-checklist workflow end to end: list the workstreams that profile triggers, the request items inside each one, and where in each workstream a red-flag escalation would fire. Then run the same request for a deal type the file has almost certainly never described — a mineral rights transfer between two private holders — and be explicit about which workstreams you invented, which you refused to invent, and why.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what would it take to add a new deal type to a skill like this — a whole new workstream template, or just one more line in the file — and how would you tell whether the change actually held under a second run?
